item.title: Bureau of Women’s Affairs is accepting domestic violence grant applications
item.description: The Guam Bureau of Women’s Affairs is accepting proposals from qualified organizations seeking federal funding for programs addressing domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking. The funding is available through the U.S. Department of Justice’s Services, Training, Officers and Prosecutors (STOP) Violence Against Women Formula Grant Program. Guam was awarded nearly $668,000 un
item.content:encoded:
The Guam Bureau of Women’s Affairs is accepting proposals from qualified organizations seeking federal funding for programs addressing domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking.

The funding is available through the U.S. Department of Justice’s Services, Training, Officers and Prosecutors (STOP) Violence Against Women Formula Grant Program. Guam was awarded nearly $668,000 under the program in fiscal year 2024.

Eligible applicants include local criminal justice agencies, such as law enforcement agencies, prosecutors, and courts, 501(c)(3) nonprofit victim-service organizations, including faith-based and community-based organizations, and local violence or sexual assault coalitions.

Organizations must demonstrate expertise in addressing domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking. Applicants proposing new projects must also explain the need for their proposed program, identify gaps in existing services, and show how their work would complement services already available in the community.

Grant funding may support existing programs or new initiatives that meet program guidelines. Eligible projects include victim services and efforts to strengthen law enforcement and justice system responses to violence against women.

Organizations proposing new projects must submit completed applications by 4 p.m. Nov. 20. Existing grant recipients seeking continued funding must also complete requirements to maintain their funding.

For application materials, submission requirements, or questions, contact the Bureau of Women’s Affairs at (671) 475-9178 or email gcofpo@guam.gov .

item.title: Julia Birn’s first solo exhibition explores chronic illness through art

item.content:encoded:
The Guam Museum Café Gallery will host “ Chewing on Static ,” the first solo exhibition by multidisciplinary artist and graphic designer Julia Birn, with the opening reception from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Oct. 24.

Birn, a recent graduate of the Savannah College of Art and Design, lives with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and dysautonomia, a broad umbrella term for any malfunction of the autonomic nervous system, which controls automatic body functions like heart rate and blood pressure. Her main diagnosis also includes postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, or POTS, a specific, common type of dysautonomia defined by an abnormal jump in heart rate. Her experiences with chronic illness inform her artwork and the exhibit, which explores uncertainty through abstraction, fragmentation, and limited color palettes.

Birn said discussing chronic illness can help people better understand the conditions of those who live with chronic illness and raise awareness.

“I’m very open to talking about what chronic illnesses I have because talking about it is how we learn more about it,” Birn said. “We learn how people deal with it. It helps get awareness to the situations and the illnesses.”

She also hopes the exhibition encourages people to consider art as a way to express experiences, like she does, beyond happiness and positive moments.

“Because art is supposed to be expressive. It doesn’t need to focus on just the happy moments or fun times,” Birn said. “And I think pushing that perspective will really expand people’s knowledge of art and how they feel towards it, and I feel like that’s needed here.”

The exhibit will remain on view through Dec. 1.

The Guam Museum is open Tuesday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. and Saturdays from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.

item.title: CNMI residents push back against proposed utility increases
item.description: Ratepayers and elected officials voiced opposition this week to the Commonwealth Utilities Corp.'s proposal to raise utility rates, as the Commonwealth Public Utilities Commission (CUC) concluded public hearings on Saipan and Tinian and prepared for a final hearing on Rota. The CUC is seeking approval for a three-year increase in electric, water and wastewater base rates, as well as a temporary Ty
item.content:encoded:
Ratepayers and elected officials voiced opposition this week to the Commonwealth Utilities Corp.'s proposal to raise utility rates, as the Commonwealth Public Utilities Commission (CUC) concluded public hearings on Saipan and Tinian and prepared for a final hearing on Rota.

The CUC is seeking approval for a three-year increase in electric, water and wastewater base rates, as well as a temporary Typhoon Restoration Surcharge to help recover costs associated with storm-related infrastructure repairs.

The public hearing process began Monday on Saipan and continued Tuesday.

On Saipan, residents, ratepayers and public officials expressed concerns about the financial burden the proposed increases would place on households and businesses already coping with high living costs.

Several speakers urged regulators to reject the proposal, arguing that customers should not be asked to pay more unless utility service and reliability improve.

The final public hearing was scheduled for Wednesday evening on Rota.

James Sirok, legal counsel for the CPUC, said a hearing administrator will prepare a report summarizing public comments and testimony from all hearings. The report will be published for an additional 10-day public comment period.

The petition is scheduled to be presented to CPUC commissioners on Nov. 18 for deliberation. Sirok said the commission is expected to issue its decision on Nov. 20.

CPUC is the independent regulatory agency responsible for reviewing and approving utility rate changes in the CNMI.

item.title: Russia releases imprisoned U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard following Trump's request
item.description: Russian President Vladimir Putin says he has freed an American, Stephen Hubbard, from a Russian prison following a request from President Trump. The announcement came as talks got underway between Putin and White House envoy Steve Witkoff focused on U.S. efforts to end the war in Ukraine.
item.content:encoded:
Russian President Vladimir Putin says he has freed an American, Stephen Hubbard, from a Russian prison following a request from President Trump.

The announcement came as talks got underway between Putin and White House envoy Steve Witkoff focused on U.S. efforts to end the war in Ukraine.

The 74-year-old Stephen Hubbard of Michigan was detained by Russian forces in eastern Ukraine in 2022 and later sentenced — after a closed trial in 2024 — to nearly seven years in prison, for serving as a mercenary in the Ukrainian army.

As talks with Witkoff got underway in Russia's former imperial capital of Saint Petersburg, Putin announced Hubbard had been released and was already at Pulkovo Airport in St. Petersburg.

Prior to the talks, Trump said he had asked Putin to release Hubbard, whom the U.S. had formally designated wrongfully detained under the Biden administration.

Hubbard's release comes as Trump has lifted some sanctions on Moscow — and openly criticized Ukraine — amid U.S. efforts to negotiate an end to the war.

item.title: 2025 policing trend: Fewer serious crimes, more minor arrests
item.description: Arrests for low-level crimes, including vagrancy and drug possession, rose in the U.S. from 2024 to 2025 even as rates of violent crime including homicide plummeted to historic national lows , according to a new analysis of federal data from the criminal justice and immigration reforms advocacy group FWD.us. item.content:encoded:
Arrests for low-level crimes, including vagrancy and drug possession, rose in the U.S. from 2024 to 2025 even as rates of violent crime including homicide plummeted to historic national lows , according to a new analysis of federal data from the criminal justice and immigration reforms advocacy group FWD.us.

Zoë Towns, the executive director of FWD.us , spoke to NPR ahead of the report's release on Wednesday.

"This increase signals a really troubling return to some of the extreme law and order policies that defined the American criminal justice system during the 80s and the 90s," Towns said, referring to the era's tough-on-crime policies , including mandatory minimum prison sentences , that led to a massive rise in incarceration in the U.S. for decades.

The report analyzes publicly available FBI and immigration arrest data and does not include details of whether charges were dropped or if people served any time in jail or prison.

Still, Towns said, "An arrest has life-changing consequences for the person involved and for their family. It can mean days or months in jail. It can mean a lost job. It can mean missed rent or a missed mortgage payment," and can mean families separated, she said.

A representative for the FBI didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on this analysis.

Four states, California, Hawaii, Nevada and Arizona, accounted for over half the increase in vagrancy arrests, according to the report. The legal definition of vagrancy is "roaming from place to place without a permanent job, home, or material resources." In practice, it is disproportionately enforced against people experiencing homelessness.

FWD.us found arrests for vagrancy were up 44% (22,769 in 2024 to 32,728 in 2025).

Two demographic groups made up the majority of arrests: Asian Americans, as well as Native Hawaiian and other Pacific Islanders. Although AANHPI people make up only about 7% of the US population, they accounted for 17% of the increase in vagrancy arrests, largely in Hawaii, according to FWD.us

Marijuana possession arrests went up 6%, mainly in Southern states that have not yet legalized the drug. The report showed there were 190,182 arrests in 2024 and 201,273 a year later.

There was a stark racial disparity between those arrested for marijuana possession: Black people accounted for 83% of the national increase in marijuana arrests in 2025 and nearly half of all cannabis arrests were of Black people (45%).

Arrests for possession of drugs other than marijuana rose marginally between 2024 to 2025. The report found a national increase of 3% in arrests or 508,087 in 2024 and 523,520 in 2025.

This increase appears to be tied to the unraveling of policies that decriminalized drug possession in some states.

Voters in California (which saw the biggest jump in arrests for drug possession) back in 2024 voted to roll back a measure that had reclassified drug possession from a felony to a misdemeanor. Proposition 36, approved by voters, increased criminal penalties for repeat thieves and drug users. FWD.us says drug possession arrests rose by over 14,000 in a single year following its passage.

That same year Oregon similarly reinstated a policy that made simple drug possession a criminal offense again. That resulted in a 39% increase (2,205) in non-marijuana drug possession arrests.

The report also highlights the vast increase (188%) in arrests for immigration violations in that time — a trend NPR has previously covered . In 2024, there were a reported 109,936 immigration violation arrests. A year later, in 2025, those arrests totaled 316,304.

FWD.us ties the increases, in part, to changes at the federal level.

The data reviewed by FWD.us covers the first full year of President Trump's second term in office. In that time the administration leaned on a tough-on-crime message.

It supercharged its deportation efforts, arresting hundreds of thousands nationwide — many of whom had no criminal convictions. Millions of federal dollars have also been sent to local police through the 287(g) program, which allows local police to make immigration arrests.

FWD believes federal deployments of immigration officers and the National Guard may have also led to increased policing and subsequently more arrests.

In summer 2025, Trump claimed American cities including Washington, D.C., were suffering from a "crime emergency" — despite data showing violent crime in the city were at a record low in 2024. He sent hundreds of National Guard troops to the city.

FWD.us found that arrests in D.C. for marijuana possession "more than doubled" following the Trump administration's deployment of National Guard into the city.

Vagrancy arrests may also be tied to actions by the Supreme Court, according to FWD's report. Two years ago, the judges ruled that cities can ban people from sleeping and camping in public places. The ruling allowed Oregon and dozens of other Western localities to limit where individuals living in cars, parks and other encampments stayed.

Insha Rahman, president and director of the criminal justice reform nonprofit Vera Institute, says there are still "incredibly positive trends" showing crime across the board is down.

Adult arrests for drug crimes peaked in 2006 at about 1.7 million, more than 2.5 times the number recorded in 1980.

Rahman says this decrease "speaks to the resilience of states and localities that have continued to double down and invest in what works." Vera was not involved in the FWD.us report.

That includes investing in treatment and diversion programs that offer assistance to people struggling with addiction, community violence intervention programs, youth services, counseling and alternative response programs.

item.title: Expecting a baby? 5 tips to help you prepare for pregnancy costs
item.description: As Grace Griffin and her husband were welcoming their long-awaited baby — a daughter — Griffin found herself worried about looming medical bills and unsure whether the family could pay for the care needed. "This whole experience has me wondering (keeping me up at night, actually): Can we ever afford to have another child?"
item.content:encoded:
As Grace Griffin and her husband were welcoming their long-awaited baby — a daughter — Griffin found herself worried about looming medical bills and unsure whether the family could pay for the care needed.

"This whole experience has me wondering (keeping me up at night, actually): Can we ever afford to have another child?"

Grace and Daniel Griffin, both 26, knew money would be tight once they had their first child. So, even before the Calumet, Mich., couple tried to conceive, they began crunching the numbers to figure out the cost of pregnancy.

"We wanted to save up enough to pay for those medical bills right away, if possible," Grace said.

But the cost estimator that she found linked to her UnitedHealthcare student plan asked for medical billing codes for each procedure that Grace was likely to receive. That's information she didn't have.

So, she kept digging until she found the Summary of Benefits and Coverage information on the health plan's website, which estimated out-of-pocket costs for a routine pregnancy and delivery at about $2,700.

"We thought, 'OK, that's doable,'" she said. "We should be able to save up that much and pay for that out of pocket."

But as the expenses piled up, it was clear the estimate wasn't even close.

Early in the pregnancy, Grace met her $500 deductible, the out-of-pocket cost she had to pay before insurance pitched in. Her plan also required her to pay 20% coinsurance for in-network care. This meant that for every $100 billed for things like routine blood work and other needed care, she was on the hook for $20.

"When I started getting lab work is when we started realizing expenses would add up quickly," Grace said. Routine blood tests to check iron levels or for gestational diabetes were a couple of hundred dollars every visit, she said.

In June, after what Grace described as a routine pregnancy and delivery, the couple welcomed their daughter. Then the Griffins received an "explanation of benefits" notice that showed the hospital charged about $18,000 for the delivery, with the family on the hook for a sizable portion.

"I thought, 'Oh no, it's going to be a lot,'" she said. "Much more than we budgeted for."

In early October, Grace said, her family's out-of-pocket expenses had totaled more than $9,000, over three times the general estimate published by her insurer for pregnancy-related costs.

Meanwhile, Grace and Daniel are scrambling to cover their bills.

For years, federal lawmakers have tried to remedy this issue, said Sabrina Corlette , a research professor and co-director of Georgetown University's Center on Health Insurance Reforms. To make healthcare costs more transparent and accessible to patients, Congress required insurers to provide consumers with an individualized "advanced explanation of benefits" estimating what scheduled care would cost them. The rule, part of the 2020 No Surprises Act, was due to take effect on Jan. 1, 2022, but federal regulators have yet to make that happen, despite ongoing pressure from members of Congress .

"So, it's basically 4 1/2 years since this was supposed to be available, and I think it's a source of a lot of frustration for a lot of folks," Corlette said. "People have a right under the law to know these things."

Meanwhile, she said, another change is pending. Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, long-standing maternity billing codes that bundle much of pregnancy care will be replaced with more detailed coding for prenatal care, labor, delivery and postpartum care.

The change could make it easier to see what individual services cost, but Corlette said it's not yet clear whether the change will make it easier for people trying to stick to a budget.

"I could see where it might be advantageous to the provider," she said. "But I'm not sure I'm seeing benefits to the patient."

Until out-of-pocket maternity expenses get easier to estimate, here are some tips to help you budget for the cost of pregnancy.

Ensuring your newborn has health coverage is one of the first paperwork responsibilities that parents face in the whirlwind of bringing a baby home.

Birth creates what's known as a special enrollment opportunity, meaning you don't have to wait until the annual open-enrollment period to sign up a newborn.

Many employer health plans require parents to request enrollment within 30 days of birth. Marketplace plans — for those who buy their own insurance rather than get it from an employer or the government — generally allow 60 days. Wait too long, and your baby may be left uninsured until the following year.

Michelle Critzer of Ventura, Calif., learned that lesson the hard way. She works as a sales rep and is the mother of a toddler and a newborn. Her second son, Hudson, was born in February, and Critzer missed the enrollment deadline for him. Ever since, she has been asking her insurer to make an exception — so far, without success.

"The way they set hard must-do's within 30 days of having a baby is actually insanity," she said.

The family was able to enroll Hudson in a health plan through Critzer's husband's workplace, which has a 60-day enrollment window. But that coverage is not nearly as robust as Critzer's insurance, she said. Still, she's grateful to have Hudson insured while she continues pressing her own plan to enroll him.

Budgeting for a pregnancy often begins with a tally of the expected expenses. The deductible is the amount you'll pay before much of your insurance coverage kicks in.

After that, you'll likely face copayments — fixed fees paid each time you receive service, regardless of the size of the bill.

Coinsurance is another expected expense, but as Grace discovered, it can be especially tricky to estimate. Coinsurance requires the patient to pay a percentage of the cost for each service received.

MOOP, which stands for "maximum out-of-pocket" expense, is another must-know number. Your plan's MOOP is the ceiling on what you'll pay each year for covered, in-network services (care that your health plan has contracted to pay at negotiated, lower rates).

item.title: LeBron James talks smack with Knicks fans in victorious 76ers debut
item.description: NEW YORK — LeBron James got the business from Knicks fans still gloating and riding an emotional high from an NBA championship banner celebration. As he stepped to the free-throw line for the Philadelphia 76ers early in Tuesday night's season opener, Knicks fans erupted toward James with chants of "We don't want you! We don't want you!"
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — LeBron James got the business from Knicks fans still gloating and riding an emotional high from an NBA championship banner celebration.

As he stepped to the free-throw line for the Philadelphia 76ers early in Tuesday night's season opener, Knicks fans erupted toward James with chants of "We don't want you! We don't want you!"

Such a rude reception from New Yorkers to one of the city's newest residents.

The shouts of rejection came in part because there was a plausible scenario under which James would have opened the season at Madison Square Garden in a Knicks uniform.

James and his agent, Rich Paul, had said the Knicks would have been James' first choice in free agency had New York not won its first NBA championship since 1973 last season.

The 41-year-old James got the final word as the Sixers won 106-100.

James talked smack with fans in the lower level. Yes, that was Spike Lee trying to play peacemaker.

James finished with 14 points and nine rebounds and had plenty of help in getting the W from new Sixers and holdovers. Tyrese Maxey scored 28 points, Jaylen Brown had 19, Joel Embiid had 13 points and 11 rebounds, and the Sixers ruined the Knicks' championship party.

A good night in New York totally spoiled? Not quite, according to James.

"I wouldn't say that," James said. "It was a great night for New York fans. Fifty-plus years. I was a part of that at one point where we hadn't won a major championship in Cleveland in over 50 years. The fans will never forget this moment."

James' first basket for the Sixers was not nearly as memorable. He took a feed from Embiid in the paint and went up strong for an uncontested right-handed layup.

Just two points. Just one bucket of what the Sixers expect to be many, many more over the next two seasons as the NBA's career scoring leader opened his record 24th season.

Embiid appeared to wonder during the national anthem where the Knicks' championship banner was hanging in the rafters as James sat nearby on the bench with his head bowed and hands clasped.

The banner was indeed raised in a pregame ceremony.

It's the same kind of celebration the 76ers expect James, Embiid and the rest of a stout starting lineup to deliver on opening night next season.

It's the thrill of the chase, to end a championship drought — much like he did to break that drought in Cleveland — that in part drives James to keep playing after racking up a list of accomplishments unrivaled by his peers.

The Sixers got a first look at the potent lineup they put together this summer in hopes of winning their first title since 1983. James and a fellow All-Star in Brown started alongside holdovers Embiid, Maxey and VJ Edgecombe.

There are some questions about how that All-Star starting four plus Edgecombe will coexist when all have been the primary ballhandlers on their respective teams in the past. Who gets the ball in crunch time? Who has to sacrifice the most? Who has the most to gain?

Watching the answers unfold in real time will be fascinating for the Sixers and their fans.

The chemistry looked strong throughout the night. James hit Brown cutting to the basket to earn the assist on the former Celtics star's first points with the Sixers. The Sixers closed the third quarter with an 11-0 run, capped by Brown's second straight 3-pointer that came at the buzzer and gave Philadelphia an 83-76 lead.

The offseason all the way through the countdown to the Sixers' home opener Thursday against Cleveland has been a swirl of excitement in Philadelphia. James jerseys are flying off the racks. Murals of him have popped up all over the city. He drew more than 10,000 fans to a public scrimmage and preseason games were sold out. There's a fascination with his helicopter rides from the Sixers' facility in New Jersey to New York.

Even his younger teammates admitted to being a bit awestruck when they first met James.

The Sixers entered the Garden almost unrecognizable from when they played there in early May in a second-round playoff series. They lost twice in New York and the Knicks finished the sweep in Philadelphia.

The Sixers loaded up with talent and pushed the payroll so they could challenge the Knicks.

"It's certainly been fun these first few weeks," coach Nick Nurse said. "These guys have been really great."

There's not much left for James to accomplish, except win that fifth ring.
